tasks.problem_solved: Perform indexed selection, gather elements along an axis, scatter values by index, or take elements along a dimension for advanced indexing and rearrangement.
tasks.mental_trigger: I need fine-grained selection or scatter semantics using index tensors.
tasks.syntax:
torch.index_select(input, dim, index)
torch.gather(input, dim, index)
torch.scatter(input, dim, index, src)
torch.take_along_dim(input, indices, dim)
important_parameters: index / indices — integer tensors specifying positions.
important_params: index / indices — integer tensors specifying positions.
tasks.return_value: New tensors representing selected/gathered results or mutated tensor for scatter (scatter may be in-place when using underscore variants).
tasks.example:
import torch
t = torch.tensor([,])[^4][^1][^2][^3]
idx = torch.tensor()[^1]
g = torch.gather(t, 1, idx.unsqueeze(0))
tasks.use_when: Implementing advanced indexing, batched gather operations, or scatter-accumulate patterns.
tasks.avoid_when: Simple slicing or boolean indexing suffices; these APIs are for index-driven operations.
gotchas: Shapes of index and input must align per API contract — mismatches raise errors.
gather/scatter semantics differ subtly; gather reads from input, scatter writes into output.
scatter may be in-place and can overwrite data unexpectedly.
take_along_dim introduced for clearer semantics in some versions — check compatibility.
tasks.performance_notes: Index-heavy operations can be memory- and compute-intensive; try to batch indices and minimize Python-level loops.
tasks.framework_migration_notes: NumPy: numpy.take_along_axis and advanced indexing map closely; TensorFlow has tf.gather, tf.scatter_nd analogs.
tasks.version_compatibility: No significant changes in modern PyTorch releases.

tasks.problem_solved: Perform elementwise arithmetic with options for functional or in-place updates for memory efficiency.
tasks.mental_trigger: I need to compute arithmetic between tensors or update tensors in-place to reduce allocations.
tasks.syntax:
torch.add(input, other, *, out=None) / torch.Tensor.add
torch.add_(tensor, other)  \# in-place variant
(similar for sub, mul, div and their in-place counterparts)
important_parameters: alpha / broadcasting rules — scale factor for some ops.
dtype promotion behavior — implicit casting rules.
important_params: alpha / broadcasting rules — scale factor for some ops.
dtype promotion behavior — implicit casting rules.
tasks.return_value: A tensor containing elementwise results; in-place variants modify the left-hand operand.
tasks.example:
import torch
a = torch.ones(3)
b = torch.tensor()[^2][^3][^1]
c = a + b
a.add_(b)
tasks.use_when: Basic arithmetic, incremental updates to buffers, and avoiding intermediate allocations.
tasks.avoid_when: Autograd history must be preserved in specific ways — in-place ops can complicate gradient computation.
gotchas: In-place ops can break autograd when they modify values needed for gradient computation.
Broadcasting rules may cause implicit expansion leading to larger allocations.
Dtype promotion can silently change dtype (e.g., int + float → float).
Using out= with overlapping memory may produce undefined behavior.
tasks.performance_notes: In-place operations reduce allocations but must be used cautiously with autograd and view-sharing semantics.
tasks.framework_migration_notes: NumPy users: in-place operators (+=) behave similarly but watch broadcasting and dtype rules.
tasks.tensorflow_equivalent: tf.add, tf.math.add, in-place semantics are not typical in TensorFlow; use variables with assign_add for mutation.
tasks.framework_equivalent: tf.add, tf.math.add, in-place semantics are not typical in TensorFlow; use variables with assign_add for mutation.
tasks.version_compatibility: No significant changes in modern PyTorch releases.

tasks.problem_solved: Perform matrix and batch-matrix multiplications with appropriate dispatch for 2D and batched tensors.
tasks.mental_trigger: I need efficient dense matrix or batched matrix multiplication on tensors.
tasks.syntax:
torch.matmul(input, other)
torch.mm(mat1, mat2)  \# 2-D only
torch.bmm(batch1, batch2)  \# 3-D batched matmul
important_parameters: out — optional preallocated output in some variants.
important_params: out — optional preallocated output in some variants.
tasks.return_value: A tensor with product results; implementations dispatch to optimized BLAS/CUDA kernels.
tasks.example:
import torch
a = torch.randn(3,4)
b = torch.randn(4,5)
c = torch.matmul(a,b)
tasks.use_when: Linear algebra, dense layers, and batched linear operations.
tasks.avoid_when: Sparse-dense matmul needed; use specialized sparse APIs.
gotchas: Dimension mismatch errors are common if ranks/shapes are incorrect.
matmul semantics differ across 1-D/2-D/ND inputs (e.g., vector-matrix behavior).
Data layout and dtype (float16 vs float32) affect kernel availability and performance.
Large batched matmul may require memory planning to avoid OOM.
tasks.performance_notes: Dispatches to highly-optimized BLAS/CUDA kernels; ensure correct dtype/device to utilize GPU backends.
tasks.framework_migration_notes: NumPy: numpy.matmul and numpy.dot map closely; TensorFlow: tf.matmul.
tasks.version_compatibility: No significant changes in modern PyTorch releases.

tasks.problem_solved: Compute reductions across specified axes to produce aggregated statistics or indices.
tasks.mental_trigger: I need sums, means, extrema, or argmax across dimensions for metrics or pooling.
tasks.syntax:
torch.sum(input, dim=None, keepdim=False)
torch.mean(input, dim=None, keepdim=False)
torch.max(input, dim=None, keepdim=False)
torch.min(input, dim=None, keepdim=False)
torch.argmax(input, dim=None, keepdim=False)
important_parameters: dim — axis or axes for reduction.
keepdim — whether to retain reduced dims.
important_params: dim — axis or axes for reduction.
keepdim — whether to retain reduced dims.
tasks.return_value: Scalar or tensor reduced along requested dimensions; dtype may be promoted during accumulation.
tasks.example:
import torch
t = torch.randn(3,4)
s = torch.sum(t, dim=1)
tasks.use_when: Metric computation, pooling, and statistical summaries.
tasks.avoid_when: You need elementwise outputs; reductions change tensor rank.
gotchas: Accumulation dtype can overflow for narrow integer types; specify dtype for safety.
max/min return values and indices variants have different signatures.
Reductions on non-contiguous tensors work but may incur copies.
argmax returns indices with dtype torch.long.
tasks.performance_notes: Reductions are implemented efficiently but can be memory-bound on large tensors; prefer in-place reductions over materializing intermediate large tensors.
tasks.framework_migration_notes: Matches NumPy reduce semantics; TensorFlow equivalents exist via tf.reduce_* functions.
tasks.version_compatibility: No significant changes in modern PyTorch releases.

tasks.problem_solved: Select elements conditionally or construct coordinate grids for indexing and positional encodings.
tasks.mental_trigger: I need to pick values by condition or build coordinate matrices for spatial operations.
important_parameters: x, y — tensors or scalars for selection.
indexing — 'xy' or 'ij' to control axis ordering.
important_params: x, y — tensors or scalars for selection.
indexing — 'xy' or 'ij' to control axis ordering.
tasks.return_value: torch.where returns a tensor selected elementwise from x or y; meshgrid returns N-D coordinate tensors.
tasks.example:
import torch
cond = torch.tensor([True, False])
out = torch.where(cond, torch.tensor(), torch.tensor())[^1]
x = torch.linspace(0,1,3)
X,Y = torch.meshgrid(x, x, indexing='xy')
tasks.use_when: Masking, conditional computation, or building coordinate frames for image ops.
tasks.avoid_when: You only need boolean indexing (use masked_select) or simple broadcasting arithmetic.
gotchas: where requires shapes compatible for broadcasting.
meshgrid indexing parameter changes axis order; mismatches cause subtle bugs.
where with mixed dtypes may upcast results.
Large meshgrids allocate O(N^2) memory for 2D cases.
tasks.performance_notes: where is efficient for elementwise selection; meshgrid can be memory-intensive for high-resolution grids.
tasks.framework_migration_notes: NumPy equivalents: numpy.where, numpy.meshgrid; TensorFlow has tf.where and tf.meshgrid.
tasks.version_compatibility: No significant changes in modern PyTorch releases.

tasks.problem_solved: Create a view that broadcasts an existing tensor across larger dimensions without allocating new storage.
tasks.mental_trigger: I need to broadcast a smaller tensor to a larger shape without copying data.
important_parameters: sizes — desired expanded shape (must be compatible via broadcasting).
important_params: sizes — desired expanded shape (must be compatible via broadcasting).
tasks.return_value: A view that behaves as if expanded to target shape; does not allocate storage but may restrict writable semantics.
tasks.example:
import torch
t = torch.tensor()[^3][^2][^1]
e = t.expand(3,3)
tasks.use_when: Broadcasting constants or parameters across batch dimensions cheaply.
tasks.avoid_when: You need a real allocated tensor (use repeat) or need to write to the expanded tensor.
gotchas: Expanded tensors are **views** with stride 0 in expanded dims; in-place writes are not allowed.
expand cannot add new memory-backed dimensions that require distinct storage.
Using expand on non-broadcast-compatible shapes raises errors.
Some ops do not accept expanded tensors as writable outputs.
tasks.performance_notes: No allocation; very cheap and ideal for read-only broadcasted operations.
tasks.framework_migration_notes: NumPy's broadcasting uses views implicitly; expand provides an explicit view API in PyTorch.
tasks.version_compatibility: No significant changes in modern PyTorch releases.

tasks.problem_solved: Create a new tensor by repeating elements along specified dimensions, allocating new storage.
tasks.mental_trigger: I need a fully materialized repeated tensor for indexing or writable buffers.
important_parameters: sizes — repeat multipliers for each dimension.
important_params: sizes — repeat multipliers for each dimension.
tasks.return_value: A newly allocated tensor with repeated copies of the original data.
tasks.example:
import torch
t = torch.tensor()[^2][^1]
r = t.repeat(2,1)  \# shape (2,2)
tasks.use_when: You require explicit allocation of repeated patterns or writable repeated data.
tasks.avoid_when: You only need read-only broadcast behavior (use expand).
gotchas: repeat allocates memory proportional to the repeated size — can be large.
Repeated data is independent copies; modifying result does not affect source.
Using repeat with large multipliers may cause OOM.
repeat requires matching ranks or prepending singleton dims as needed.
tasks.performance_notes: Memory and allocation heavy compared to expand; avoid when expand suffices.
tasks.framework_migration_notes: NumPy: numpy.repeat and numpy.tile provide related functionality.
tasks.version_compatibility: No significant changes in modern PyTorch releases.

tasks.problem_solved: Move tensors across devices and change numeric precision for performance or device compatibility.
tasks.mental_trigger: I need to place tensors on a specific device or change dtype/precision for compute.
tasks.syntax:
tensor.to(device=None, dtype=None, non_blocking=False, copy=False)
tensor.cpu(), tensor.cuda(device=None, non_blocking=False), tensor.to(torch.float32), tensor.half(), tensor.to(torch.bfloat16)
important_parameters: dtype — target dtype (torch.float32, torch.float16, torch.bfloat16, etc.).
non_blocking — whether copy may be asynchronous for pinned memory.
copy — force a copy even if already matching dtype/device.
important_params: dtype — target dtype (torch.float32, torch.float16, torch.bfloat16, etc.).
non_blocking — whether copy may be asynchronous for pinned memory.
copy — force a copy even if already matching dtype/device.
tasks.return_value: A tensor on the requested device and dtype; may be a view when only dtype/format-preserving operations are performed but usually returns a new tensor when moving devices or changing dtype.
tasks.example:
import torch
t = torch.randn(3,3)
g = t.cuda()
f = g.float()
h = f.to('cpu', non_blocking=True)
tasks.use_when: Preparing tensors for device-specific computation, optimizing memory footprint with lower precision, or converting for interoperability.
tasks.avoid_when: Automatic implicit device moves are cheaper for prototyping but expensive in production; prefer explicit placement.
gotchas: to(cuda) performs a device transfer that allocates GPU memory; ensure device has capacity.
non_blocking only helps when source is pinned host memory.
Casting to lower precision can change numerical behavior and support of kernels.
Using .cuda() without specifying device in multi-GPU contexts can target unexpected GPU.
tasks.performance_notes: Device transfers and dtype casts are expensive; minimize host-device copies and prefer appropriate dtype and placement from creation time.
tasks.framework_migration_notes: NumPy has no device semantics; TensorFlow uses device contexts and tf.cast for dtype conversion.
tasks.tensorflow_equivalent: tf.cast, with device placement via with tf.device(...)
tasks.framework_equivalent: tf.cast, with device placement via with tf.device(...)
tasks.version_compatibility: No significant changes in modern PyTorch releases.
